newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A -- Balanced budget, Part VI.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A -- Balanced budget, Part VI.

text.p: Following are excerpts from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's question-and-answer session the Senate Banking Committee with after the second day of his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Greenspan in response to a Senator's question about balancing the budget: "One of the immediate aspects of a surplus, if it looks as though it is a structural surplus, will be very difficult to do beyond the year 2000. But even for the intermediate period, it would do two things: One, it would indicate that the Congress is moving in the direction in which the big bulge in potential deficits for the second decade and beyond are not likely to occur because you are addressing it in advance. Secondly, nominal long-term interest rates have come down considerably from their peaks in the early 1980s. But we are still above where we were in the 50s and 60s because there is a significant inflation premium built into long-term interest rates. There is still a belief that the American government is not going to be able to handle inflation in the manner which one can presume -- a non-inflationary environment is here to stay ... If we go lower it means much greater capital investment, much more intensive use of our resources, (and) much lower mortgage interest rates for home ownership. There are an awful lot of positives which spill out -- which gives you a sense of a virtuous economic cycle where you get lower long-term interest rates, increased capital investment, increased productivity, increased growth and lower inflation. It's a process which we should endeavor to foster and a major way of doing it is to recognize that passing the zero budget deficit line doesn't mean you should stop there. The benefits that are achieved from going from high budget deficits to low budget deficits to balance continue as you move over that line into surpluses and I would think understanding that process and fostering that process ... would be something of considerable value to the future of the country."
